 TO THE HONORABLE COMMISSIONERS:

           Intervenors Frederick Bartlett Wulff, Sr. and Frederick B. Wulff, Jr., on behalf of Wulff

Bluff Creek Ranch, Ltd., and Samuel HV Abell, on behalf of Abell Ranches, LP (collectively, the

“Brady Creek Intervenors”) (Party No. 574) file this Reply to the Exceptions to the Proposal for

Decision (“PFD”), and in support thereof would respectfully show the following:

I.         INTRODUCTION

           This proceeding involves the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC

and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (collectively, “Applicants”) to amend their

Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation

765-kV Transmission Line Project (the “Project”), a proposed high-voltage transmission line

spanning approximately 223 miles across fifteen Texas counties. Together with the Big Hill

Substation to Sand Lake Switch 765-kV Transmission Line Project (Docket No. 59182), the

Project comprises Import Path 2 of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”).

           The ALJs Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) recommendation that the Commission deny the

Application was principally based on the issue of need for this Project: the ALJs concluded that

Applicants failed to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation,

convenience, or safety of the public under PURA § 37.056. 1 This was the correct conclusion.

           BCI’s Reply Brief set out BCI’s position that Applicants failed to establish need for Import

Path 2, that two of the three 765-kV import paths are sufficient to serve demand through 2038, and

that Import Path 2 should be denied. 2 The PFD’s need findings reached the same conclusion.

           The Applicants, PUC Commission Staff (“Staff”), and Delaware Basin Midstream LLC

(“DBM”) filed Exceptions to the PFD’s need findings on September 2, 2026, 3 each asking the

Commission to reject the ALJs’ recommendation and instead find that Import Path 2 is necessary

under PURA § 37.056(a). BCI’s Reply responds to the need-related arguments raised in those

Exceptions.

          The ALJs identified four independent reasons why Applicants failed to establish need for

Import Path 2: (1) Applicants did not establish the need for Import Path 2 separate and apart from

the three 765-kV import paths comprising the PBRP; (2) the PBRP’s underlying projected loads,

because of changed circumstances, do not establish need; (3) Applicants failed to prove that

sufficient power is available at Bell County East to serve Import Path 2’s stated function of

transmitting power west into the Permian Basin; and (4) intervenors submitted credible evidence

of an alternative, new, and planned gas generation in the Permian Basin that the Commission

should consider before committing to Import Path 2. 4 Any one of the four bases, standing alone,

is sufficient to deny the Application on need grounds. 5

App.—Austin Nov. 9, 1994) (not designated for publication) (affirming denial of a CCN for lack of need where the
record contained findings that cut both for and against necessity, and holding that “if there is evidence to support either

            As shown below, none of the Exceptions raised against the ALJs’ findings identify evidence

that disproves any of these four independent grounds. The PFD’s findings on need rest on

admissions by Applicants’ own witnesses, on Staff’s witness John Poole, and on documentary

evidence, including the Commission’s orders. None of the parties’ Exceptions dispute the

evidentiary record the ALJs relied upon in reaching their determination that need has not been met

for this Project. What the Exceptions actually attempt to dispute is the weight and legal significance

the ALJs assigned to that undisputed evidence. The ALJs did not err in that assessment.

           The Commission should overrule any exceptions concerning the subject of need, adopt

PFD’s Finding of Fact and Conclusions of Law as stated, and deny the Application for this Project.

           Finally, in an alternative finding, the ALJs determined that, should the Commission

approve the Application, Route 894 best meets the routing criteria set forth under PURA

§ 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and PUC Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B). 6 This Reply also responds to

Staff’s routing Exception in Section III. As set out below, should a routing decision be reached,

either Route 392 or Route 410 best satisfy the statutory and regulatory routing criteria. 7




an affirmative or a negative finding, we must uphold the agency decision,” because “it is immaterial that some findings
or portions of the record weigh against an agency’s decision if other findings and record evidence support that
decision”); Hammack v. Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex., 131 S.W.3d 713, 725–26 (Tex. App.—Austin 2004) (holding that
under the substantial evidence rule, courts “presume that the Commission’s order is supported by substantial evidence
and appellants have the burden to overcome this presumption,” that “substantial evidence” means “such relevant
evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion of fact,” and that “the Commission’s
decision need only be supported by substantial evidence, i.e., ‘whether some reasonable basis exists in the record’ for
the agency determination”); see also Tex. Gov’t Code § 2001.174 (West) (providing that a reviewing court “may not
substitute its judgment for the judgment of the state agency on the weight of the evidence on questions committed to
agency discretion,” but “shall reverse or remand” if the agency’s findings, inferences, conclusions, or decisions are
“not reasonably supported by substantial evidence considering the reliable and probative evidence in the record as a
whole”).

 II.        BRADY CREEK INTERVENORS’ REPLY REGARDING NEED

       A. Executive Summary.

           Each Import Path 2 line has a rated capacity of 7,131 MVA, or 6,917 MW applying the

0.97 power factor used in the PBRP study.8 The PBRP’s own incremental oil-and-gas-plus-non-

large-load need is only 2,193 MW in 2030 and 4,934 MW in 2038, well within the capacity of a

single 765-kV line and comfortably within the capacity of two lines applying the N-1 reliability

standard the PBRP itself uses. 9 The demand projections Applicants cite may justify two Import

Paths to the Permian Basin. But they do not justify three. Nothing in the Exceptions filed by the

Applicants, Staff, or DBM disproves this basic arithmetic.

           If the Commission agrees with ERCOT’s own December 12, 2024 sequencing

determination that only two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030, 10 then Import

Path 2 is the clear candidate for denial. Import Path 2 is the most constrained of the three paths,

and the path for which Applicants concede no partial-build or independent-need study was ever

performed. 11 Import Paths 1 and 3 satisfy the needs Applicants and ERCOT have actually

substantiated through the HB 5066 process.

       B. The Applicants Did Not Establish the Need for Import Path 2 as Required by
          PURA.

           Applicants argue that the PBRP’s three 765-kV import paths were “designed as part of an

integrated transmission solution” and that no “partial build study” isolating Import Path 2 is

 required by PURA or Commission rule.12 Both arguments miss the point of the PFD’s holding and

the underlying concern regarding accepting Applicants’ stated justifications that need has been

established for this Project.

           The PFD did not hold that PURA or Commission rule imposes a freestanding “partial build

study” requirement. It held that HB 5066 does not make a transmission project’s inclusion in a

reliability plan a finding that the project is automatically needed, and that the necessity of any

transmission project included in the PBRP “must be independently determined by the Commission

through the lens of PURA § 37.056.” 13 That determination follows directly from Section 37.056,

which requires a showing, in each CCN proceeding, that the certificated facility is “necessary for

the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.” 14 Applicants’ own witness Jared

Gurley admitted on cross-examination that Applicants had not performed a study isolating Import

Path 2’s need individually, and that the three import paths “were studied together.” 15 Whatever

value that combined study has for ERCOT’s own regional planning purposes, it is not evidence

that Import Path 2, the specific facility for which Applicants seek a CCN amendment in this docket,

is independently necessary.

           Applicants’ reliance on the N-1-1 contingency requirement under NERC Reliability

Standard TPL-001 does not fill this gap. Mr. Gurley testified that he assumed the requirement to

study N-1-1 contingencies, which requires the ability to remove an element during modeling,

 “leads into part of the recommendation for multiple lines.” 16 As Intervenor Whitis Land

Investments argued, and as the ALJs correctly found, NERC contingency modeling can and should

inform ERCOT’s overarching regional planning, but it is not a substitute for proving project-

specific need for Import Path 2 under the PURA § 37.056(c) factors. 17 The Applicants’ and DBM’s

Exceptions do not address these issues but simply reassert that the three paths were studied as an

“integrated system,” which the PFD already accepted as true and correctly held insufficient

standing alone.

           Applicants and DBM also invoke the Commission’s orders in Docket Nos. 59029 and

59315 as having already established need for “the import paths,” including Import Path 2. 18 Those

dockets did not determine the need for Import Path 2. Docket No. 59029 concerned the Longshore

Switch–Drill Hole Switch segment of Import Path 1, and Docket No. 59315 concerned the

Dinosaur Switch–Longshore Switch segment of the same path. 19 Neither order adjudicated the

record now before the Commission in this docket.

           Former Commission Chairman Barry Smitherman’s unrebutted testimony helps confirm

why decisions on Import Path 1 do not control the need determination for Import Path 2. Chairman

Smitherman testified that “[t]he Commission’s obligation to determine if the line is needed for the

convenience and necessity of the public is different than the standard of review of need undertaken

at ERCOT,” that the Commission “should consider ERCOT’s recommendation, but it is not bound

by the results of the ERCOT process,” and that “[t]here is no harm in updating this analysis to

destruction of private property that would come with approving” Import Path 2. 20 In approving

the PBRP, the Commission expressly declined to make plan approval dispositive of need for

the individual transmission projects. Instead, the Commission required each TSP to establish

in its subsequent CCN proceeding that its proposed certificate satisfies PURA § 37.056(a)’s

statutory necessity requirement. 21

           For these reasons, the PFD correctly required Applicants to establish need for Import Path 2

on its own record, correctly found that Applicants did not perform the individualized study

necessary to do so, and correctly declined to treat the Commission’s approval of a different import

path in a different docket as substituting for that showing.

       C. The ALJs Correctly Weighed ERCOT’s PBRP Recommendation Against the
          Full Evidentiary Record.

           Applicants argue that the ALJs erred in declining to give ERCOT’s PBRP recommendation

“great weight” under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II). 22 Staff makes largely the same argument,

adding that the PFD improperly relied on the absence of ERCOT testimony, mischaracterized Staff

witness John Poole’s position, and misinterpreted ERCOT’s Far West Import GTC

recommendation. 23 None of these arguments meaningfully engage the rule’s textual predicate for

“great weight,” and each also overlooks the ALJs’ extensive analysis of the need record.

           Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) does not give ERCOT’s recommendations “great weight”

automatically. It conditions that weight on the underlying “forecasted load growth and additional

load growth.” 24 And the PFD gave two independent justifications why that predicate is not satisfied

here.

           First, 61 percent of the PBRP’s projected non-oil-and-gas load is confirmed by a letter from

a transmission service provider officer (55 percent) or wholly unconfirmed (6 percent), rather than

confirmed by binding contract or demonstrable, quantifiable need. 25 In 2025, after “performing

historical analysis on large load realization” rates, ERCOT sought, and the Commission itself

granted, a Good Cause Exception discounting officer-letter loads to 55.4 percent and data-center

loads to 49.8 percent of forecasted megawatts, finding “good cause” because of “the recent actual

experience... of previously forecasted loads coming into service at lower megawatt level than

initially claimed.” 26 Applying that Commission-ordered adjustment to the PBRP’s own officer-

letter and unconfirmed non-oil-and-gas load yields a reduction of at least 3,571 MW, against

Import Path 2’s total capacity of only 5,270 MW. 27 Applicants do not dispute this reduction, but

state only that they cannot speculate how it would affect the PBRP’s 2030 and 2038 estimates.28

That is not an answer. Applicants know exactly how much of their own submitted load falls into

each confirmation category, and they have never explained why a reduction of this size leaves the

Import Path 2 Projects still needed. 29

            Second, ERCOT never made a credibility finding regarding the S&P Global study

underlying the PBRP’s oil-and-gas load forecast. ERCOT used that study because HB 5066

directed it to implement that study; the PFD correctly recognized that complying with a statutory

directive to use a particular study is not the same as ERCOT endorsing that study’s forecasts as

credible. 30 Under ERCOT’s own Nodal Protocols, “substantiated load” for an independent third-

party forecast requires that ERCOT have “deemed [it] credible.” 31 No such finding exists in this

record, and Applicants’ Exceptions do not identify one; they instead argue only that ERCOT

continued to include all three 765-kV import paths as base assumptions in its own system models

after adopting the 2025 RTP methodology. 32 However, that is a statement about the PBRP’s

continued inclusion in ERCOT’s planning base case, not a statement that ERCOT deemed the

underlying S&P Global forecast credible.

           Staff’s argument that the PFD improperly relied on the absence of ERCOT testimony

misreads the PFD. 33 The ALJs did not hold that “great weight” deference requires ERCOT

testimony; they held that the underlying load forecast is not “substantiated by quantifiable evidence

of projected load growth” as the rule independently requires, regardless of who sponsors that

evidence. 34 Applicants decide what evidence to present in their direct case, and Applicants’ own

witness could not provide the requisite substantiation. When asked on cross-examination whether

       D. Applicants and Staff Treat ERCOT’s Recommendations as Sacrosanct Only
          When Convenient, and the Changed Circumstances and Far West Import
          GTCs Confirm the PFD’s Findings.

           Applicants’ Exceptions rest on an inconsistent premise. Applicants argue that ERCOT’s

2024 PBRP recommendation is sacrosanct, and that the Commission’s June 2025 Good Cause

Exception, which discounts officer-letter and data-center loads to reflect years of overstated

forecasts, cannot retroactively touch the PBRP’s original load figures. 41 However, Applicants do

not rest their need case on the 2024 PBRP alone. They rely on the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP, and

the April 2026 Far West Import GTC exit strategy as independent sources of “great weight” that

reaffirm the need for Import Path 2. 42

           That reliance overstates what those later documents actually show. ERCOT included the

completed 765-kV import paths as part of its “default” base case in the 2024 and 2025 Regional

Transmission Plans, but did not independently reevaluate the need for them. 43 A base assumption

is an input a planner carries forward from an earlier approval. It is not a new finding that the input

remains correct. This analytical error is compounded when assumption is stacked on assumption.

Applicants ask the Commission to treat the original recommendation as fixed against the evidence

that undercuts it, while treating every later ERCOT product built on that same evidence as fresh

proof that the original recommendation is still good.

             The same selectivity appears in how Applicants handle ERCOT’s own words. ERCOT’s

December 12, 2024 sequencing letter stated that only two of the three 765-kV import paths are

needed by 2030. 44 That statement is itself an ERCOT recommendation, presumably entitled on

Applicants’ own terms to the same “great weight” they insist upon elsewhere. Applicants would

 Rather, many of the natural, scenic, cultural, and recreational values for which a park is established

derive from the broader landscape in which the park is situated. Scenic vistas, undeveloped

horizons, wildlife habitat, ecological connectivity, dark skies, quiet soundscapes, historic settings,

and the visual character of the surrounding environment often constitute integral components of

the park experience and of the resources the park was created to protect.

       Accordingly, effective stewardship of a state park necessarily includes consideration of

external activities that may substantially alter or degrade those surrounding conditions. While the

State’s direct management authority may be limited to lands within park boundaries, the

conservation objectives reflected in Parks and Wildlife Code Chapters 13 and 26 and in the

Commission’s land-classification rules recognize that preservation of park resources is not merely

a matter of protecting a surveyed tract of land. It also requires, where reasonably possible,

protecting the environmental, scenic, and cultural context that gives those resources their meaning

and value.

       The public’s interest in a state park therefore extends beyond protection of discrete natural

features located within the park itself. Visitors come to experience landscapes, viewsheds,

ecosystems, historical settings, and recreational opportunities that frequently depend upon

conditions existing both inside and outside park boundaries. Actions that materially impair those

surrounding conditions may diminish the very resources that the State Park System was established

to conserve and present to the public.

       For that reason, preservation of the Texas State Park System is most faithfully understood

as preservation not only of park lands themselves, but also—when feasible and consistent with

governing law—of the scenic, ecological, cultural, and historical setting that contributes to the

parks’ long-term character, integrity, and public value.
